tier1.text: The axis acts as the pivot when you turn your head to the right or left. The axis is the second of the seven cervical vertebrae, the bones of the spine in the neck. The axis looks much like typical cervical vertebrae, but it has the dens, a bony part that sticks up. The atlas, the first cervical vertebra, turns around the dens when you shake your head “no.”

quotes.quote: The second cervical (C2) vertebra is called the axis, because it serves as the axis for rotation when turning the head toward the right or left.

quotes.quote: The axis resembles typical cervical vertebrae in most respects, but is easily distinguished by the dens (odontoid process), a bony projection that extends upward from the vertebral body.
quotes.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

quotes.quote: dens: bony projection (odontoid process) that extends upward from the body of the C2 (axis) vertebra
quotes.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

sentences.text: The atlas, the first cervical vertebra, turns around the dens when you shake your head “no.”

quotes.quote: For example, at the atlantoaxial joint, the first cervical (C1) vertebra (atlas) rotates around the dens, the upward projection from the second cervical (C2) vertebra (axis). This allows the head to rotate from side to side as when shaking the head “no.”
quotes.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.
